title: ASIRT says no charges in shooting death of Anthony Heffernan
article: Anthony Heffernan wasn\'t armed.
When police broke down the door of the Calgary motel room where Heffernan was staying, the 27-year-old journeyman electrician put his hands in the air.
He was holding a lighter in one hand, and an empty plastic syringe, with no tipped needle, in the other.

Police hadn\'t come to arrest a dangerous criminal. Staff at the Calgary Super 8 had called police and ambulance because they were worried that Heffernan was in medical distress. This was supposed to be a "wellness check," not a high risk takedown.
Yet 72 seconds after five police officers forced their way into his room, Anthony Heffernan was dead, shot four times in the head, neck and torso.
That was March 16, 2015.

On Monday, more than a year later, ASIRT, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, issued a press release announcing that no charges would be laid against the "subject officer" who fired those shots - despite an opinion by ASIRT that there were reasonable grounds to believe that offences under the criminal Code had been committed.

In an unprecedented move, the province\'s Crown Prosecution Service issued its own case assessment , which determined there would be no reasonable likelihood of conviction, had criminal charges been laid.

"We could not disprove that the use of force was reasonable," said Eric Tolppanen, Alberta\'s assistant deputy minister of justice, responsible for the Crown Prosecution Service, told a press conference Monday afternoon in Calgary.
But then Tolppanen went further, saying the officer who fired "had no reasonable alternatives to taking the steps that he did."
Now, those are two very different statements.

The threshold to lay criminal charges is very high. We don\'t ever want officers to be prosecuted simply in response to public outrage. And we don\'t want to prosecute people criminally for errors in judgment, for honest, good faith, mistakes.
But for the Crown to assert that this office had no reasonable alternative?

Let\'s recap the events of that tragic afternoon. Hotel staff, unable to get a response from Heffernan, called for help. At that point, to the best anyone knew, he was simply in medical or psychiatric distress. When emergency medical services arrived, they were directed by police to wait in the lobby. Through a crack in the doorway, police could see Heffernan was flushed, hyperventilating and non-responsive. They forced the door open, saying afterwards they believed the young man was in urgent need of medical intervention.

Heffernan, high on cocaine, confused, raised his hands. Police ordered him to drop the syringe. Seemingly unaware or unable to understand their orders, he didn\'t respond. One officer Tasered him, and Heffernan fell on the bed. Two other officers holstered their weapons and tried to subdue him physically, but Heffernan was flailing, trying to pull the Taser probes from his skin. He stood up and, according to some accounts, stepped or perhaps lunged towards the officers.
Another officer, the one who\'d entered the room last, fired his Taser. At the same time, the "subject officer" drew his gun and fired six shots, four of which hit Heffernan.
In all, 11 seconds elapsed between the first Taser shot and the hail of bullets.
Did the officer who killed Heffernan really have "no reasonable alternative"?
His colleagues felt no need to shoot. Only the "subject officer" discharged his firearm: six times in close quarters, putting not only Heffernan, but the other officers, at risk.

The explanation later was that the officer was afraid of being pricked by a needle, and of contracting a blood-borne disease such as hepatitis or HIV. But Heffernan had no needle to prick anyone. And he had no infectious disease. The officer who killed him imagined a dangerous scenario and responded to it. No such danger ever existed.
"It\'s just unbelievable," says Heffernan\'s mother, Irene. "If this isn\'t murder, I don\'t know what is. You knock down a door, and in 72 seconds, someone is dead?"
"What we\'re really looking for that they do make changes," says Heffernan\'s father, Patrick. "This cannot go on. You\'ve got to hold the police accountable."

The Heffernans take some comfort that the Calgary Police Service will now launch its own internal investigation - and from comments by Calgary police chief Roger Cheffin that the service will review its "use of force" training and its mental health strategy. But without a trial, without putting the police witnesses under public cross-examination, they don\'t feel there\'s been justice for Anthony - nor answers for them.

We only know Heffernan\'s name because his family had the social capacity and the media savvy to make his story public. Otherwise, ASIRT, which refuses to name those who die at the hands of police, even though that secrecy is not required by law, would have kept his identity a secret. Meantime, the officer who shot Heffernan, who has never been identified by ASIRT, has been linked by Calgary media to the fatal shooting of another mentally ill Calgary man earlier this year.

This isn\'t just a Calgary story. It should disturb all Albertans who rely on ASIRT to hold police accountable - especially since in all of ASIRT\'s history, no officer involved in a fatal incident has ever been charged.

A public fatality inquiry, sometime in the unspecified future, may provide more answers. But it won\'t assign responsibility. And it may not come in time to help prevent the next tragedy. Nor the one after that.
